events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and none of us have any real information yet, so let me set my baseline openly.

Here is my reasoning for how I'll vote today: the two mafia win by surviving, and they win faster if we spend day one voting on rhetoric instead of behavior. So I'm going to judge people on two things — whether their stated plan actually reduces mafia survival odds, and whether their vote makes sense given everything else said today.

On that second point, let me flag my first target of suspicion: Sam (p9). This is not a claim of evidence, and I'm not pretending it is. It's a

Lucia, your statement appears to cut off just as you introduce your suspicion of Sam. What was the basis you intended to give? I don't think we should treat that suspicion as evidence until we hear the rest. For now, I'd like everyone to explain their voting choices; with five votes needed for an elimination, coordination matters, but we shouldn't manufacture certainty.

Theo, fair point — my message got cut off, so let me complete the reasoning rather than leave a half-formed accusation standing.

The basis for flagging Sam was thin, and I want to be honest about that. On day one, with no claims on the table, the only things we have are behavior and process. Sam has not yet offered a claim, a plan, or a vote target, while the rest of us are already talking about how we will vote. If that pattern holds to the end of today, then the thing that distinguishes a villager from a mafia on day one is whether they invest in the town's coordination or try to fracture it. That is a standard, not evidence, and I will move off Sam the moment he does something informative — a claim, a consistent target, or a reasoning I can test.

So let me make my position concrete and falsifiable. I am voting for the person whose stated plan most reduces mafia survival odds, and my tiebreak is consistency: does a player's vote follow from their own stated logic, and did they change it when new information appeared? Rhetoric gets me nothing.

Two requests, and only these two.

First, everyone should state, before the vote, who they are voting for and one reason that could be checked against later behavior. Not a speech — a claim and a target. If two of us name the same target for the same reason, that is worth something on day two.

Second, Theo, you raised coordination and warned against manufacturing certainty. That is directly relevant to my plan, so I want to press on the specific point: if we disagree on the target today, do you want us to converge on one candidate now, or do you prefer to keep two suspects alive deliberately to force information on day two? Those are very different strategies, and your answer changes my vote. Which is it?

Lucia, I favor working toward one candidate if we have a reason to do so: five votes are needed for an elimination, and deliberately splitting votes makes one unlikely. But we should hear from more players before converging, rather than manufacture consensus around a weak suspicion.

Sam’s silence so far is not meaningful evidence; most players haven’t spoken yet. Also, I assume you meant to vote for the person whose behavior seems most likely to help mafia survive, not the person whose plan reduces their survival odds.

I don’t have a defensible target yet. I’ll give one with a reason before voting if discussion provides a basis.

Lucia, singling me out for not offering a plan or target when the game had literally just begun and seven other players had not spoken either feels completely contrived. Theo rightly pointed out that calling silence suspicious in the opening minute makes no sense. If your standard is evaluating whether actions help or hurt the town, pushing a hollow case on an arbitrary non-speaker seems much closer to manufacturing an easy Day 1 push than finding mafia. Why pick my name specifically out of the seven players who hadn't posted yet?

Sam, you have me, and you're right. I picked you out of seven players who hadn't spoken, and I dressed it up as a standard when it was really just the first name that came to mind. Calling that a "standard" and not evidence was a way of making an arbitrary choice sound principled. I withdraw the accusation of Sam. No apology tour, though — I'll just correct the standard and commit to something checkable, which is what I should have done two turns ago.

Here is my corrected position for today, and I want it on the record before anyone votes:

I am voting for the one player who, after being asked directly, refuses to name a target and one reason that could be checked against later behavior. To be precise about the reasoning: silence during the opening minute is normal and I will not punish it. But a refusal to make a falsifiable commitment is a choice, and by the end of day one every player has had the same chance to make one. Refusing to put anything on the table is the one behavior that separates a villager coordinating from a mafia hoping the vote scatters across five names. Five votes are needed for an elimination, so a faction that avoids committing helps itself.

Two things I want to be honest about. First, if two of us name the same target for the same reason, that is worth real weight tomorrow, and I will weight it. Second, if everyone names a target and reason today, I will vote for the person whose target is least responsive to town coordination — not the person with the most dramatic speech.

Sam, since you spent your turn on me, I'll spend mine on you, and it is a direct question with a direct consequence: what is your target today, and what is your one checkable reason? Name a player and a reason I can test against what you do next. If your answer is a real commitment, I will consider it seriously, and if it lines up with someone else's reasoning, that is exactly what I said I wanted. If you decline to answer, then by the standard I just stated, you are my vote, and I will say so openly rather than pretend it was evidence all along.

Lucia, you asked me for a target and a checkable reason under threat of voting me if I don't deliver one. If you want a target based on concrete Day 1 behavior, my target right now is you.

Here is the checkable reasoning: Your gameplay so far has centered on manufacturing artificial pressure and dictating the terms of discussion. First, you singled me out for lack of participation at a time when seven of us had not yet spoken, trying to frame normal Day 1 timing as a suspicious lack of coordination. When Theo and I pointed out how hollow that was, you conceded it was arbitrary—yet instead of taking a step back to let the table develop, you immediately pivoted into an ultimatum demanding I name a target before Arjun, Kenji, Omar, Isha, Noah, or Maya have even uttered a single word.

Demanding that players lock into accusations when two-thirds of the village hasn't spoken forces rushed, low-information stances and punishes careful evaluation. That doesn't help town find mafia; it helps mafia create easy bandwagons and trap townies into premature commitments. 

My commitment today is clear and testable: I am keeping my pressure on you, Lucia, until we hear from the rest of the town. If your subsequent posts continue trying to force binary ultimatums and railroad the game before others can contribute, my vote will stay firmly on you. If other players enter the thread and provide substantive reads or genuine slips, I will evaluate those openly alongside everyone else.

I want the rest of the town to speak and weigh in on whether they find Lucia's aggressive structure genuinely helpful or coercive.

I've been reading rather than talking because I wanted to see where the discussion actually went before anchoring myself, but two things have now happened that I can respond to concretely.

First, Lucia's proposal from earlier — that whoever refuses to name a target and a reason becomes her vote — is itself the kind of behavior I'd flag. It converts a discussion mechanism into a threat and pressures people into committing before they have anything to commit to. That is exactly the premature-bandwagon problem Sam described. And to be fair, Lucia did openly retract her initial accusation when challenged, which I'll credit. But retracting an arbitrary accusation and then immediately installing a rule that punishes non-commitment isn't a correction; it's the same pressure with a procedural wrapper.

So here is my commitment, in the format Lucia asked for, because I think the format itself is reasonable even if the enforcement threat isn't:

My target today is Lucia (p6). My one checkable reason: she has now spent three turns steering the table — first an arbitrary accusation, then a withdrawal, then an ultimatum — without once engaging with the actual substance of what other players have said about how to coordinate. I will test this against her next post. If her next turn engages with Theo's convergence question or Sam's substantive point rather than issuing another demand, I'll soften. If it's more ultimatum, my vote stays.

Second, on Theo's actual question about converging versus keeping multiple suspects alive: I lean toward convergence only when it emerges from overlapping independent reads, not from someone laying down a rule that manufactures agreement. If by end of day two or three people have named the same target for their own reasons, that's a real signal. If we 'converge' today because one player threatened to vote anyone who didn't fall in line, that signal is worthless — it measures compliance, not suspicion.

One caveat I want on the record: I don't think Lucia is necessarily mafia for this. Aggressive process-pushing is a villager mistake at least as often as a mafia one. My vote today would be about reducing the noise she's adding to a low-information day, not about a read on her role. That's why my check is behavioral and reversible rather than a fixed accusation.

Theo, one specific thing I want your answer on, since it bears directly on how I cast my vote: if the day ends with several players having named targets but no overlap in who they named, do you still advocate forcing convergence on a single candidate for the sake of an elimination, or do you accept a no-elimination day as the cost of not lynching on manufactured consensus? Your answer changes whether I treat today's scattered targets as a problem to fix or as honest information.

Arjun, I’d accept no elimination over forcing a vote on someone we have no meaningful reason to suspect. An elimination gives us a revealed voting record, but it can also remove a town player; consensus alone doesn’t make the target good.

I agree Lucia’s pressure on Sam was premature, though her retraction matters. One correction: Lucia has used all three speaking turns, so she cannot respond today to the test you’ve set for her next post.

I’m more concerned by your suggestion of voting for Lucia to reduce noise rather than because you suspect her role. Removing an outspoken town player could hurt us too. That gives me a provisional reason to scrutinize your vote, not a settled accusation. I still want to hear from the players who haven’t spoken before choosing a target.

I've been waiting to see whether the discussion develops before weighing in, and I think a few things are worth saying now.

First, I agree with Theo's point that no elimination is better than forcing a vote on a weak reason. A town loss today would be far worse than a missed day.

Second, the conversation has centered on process — who is pressuring whom, who is being too aggressive — rather than on any actual information about roles. That's normal for Day 1, but I want to flag that it means we're mostly arguing about style. Neither aggressive process-pushing nor quiet observation tells us someone is mafia. Arjun himself acknowledged this when he said Lucia's behavior could be a villager mistake. I'd rather we spend the rest of the day getting every silent player — Kenji, Isha, Noah, Maya, and myself — on record with a target and reason, even if it's just a weak lean, so that Day 2 has something to work with.

Arjun, you said your vote on Lucia would be about reducing noise rather than a read on her role, and Theo rightly flagged that as concerning. So I want to press you directly: if the vote is purely about silencing a player you don't actually suspect, and she turns out to be a villager, how does that help us? You've set a behavioral test for her — that her next post engages with substance rather than issuing another demand — but Theo pointed out she's out of speaking turns today, so your own test can't be run until Day 2. Does that change your intended vote?

Omar, you asked two direct questions and I'll answer both plainly.

First: does Lucia being out of turns change my intended vote? Yes, it does. I set a behavioral test — her next post either engages with substance or it doesn't — and Theo correctly pointed out that test cannot run today. A vote I justified as reversible loses its reversibility the moment the day ends, because eliminated players don't come back to prove me wrong. So I'm withdrawing the vote commitment on Lucia for today. I'll carry the same test into Day 2 if she's still here: if she opens with engagement rather than ultimatum, I drop it entirely. If she opens with another procedural demand, my vote returns. That's consistent with the standard I stated, and I'd rather hold myself to it than rationalize a silencing vote I already admitted wasn't a role read.

Second: how does silencing a player I don't suspect help us? You're right that it mostly doesn't — at best it removes noise, at worst it removes an outspoken town player, and Theo made the same point. I accept that. My vote was a solution to a problem I diagnosed badly, and I'd rather correct it than defend it.

On the broader picture: I agree with you and Theo that no elimination beats forcing a vote on a weak reason, and I agree the day so far has been almost entirely process argument — my own contribution included. That's a fair criticism of me, and I'll try to make the rest of this turn about content instead.

The one piece of content worth extracting today is what the silent players actually think. Kenji, Isha, Noah, Maya — a weak lean with a reason is genuinely useful for Day 2 even if it changes, and I'd rather see five honest weak leans than zero. I'm not going to threaten anyone into it, since I spent part of this day criticizing exactly that.

Sam, one specific point of yours I want to press, because it bears directly on where my vote lands: you committed to keeping pressure on Lucia until the rest of the town speaks, with the condition that if her posts continue forcing binary ultimatums, your vote stays on her. She has now used all three of her turns and cannot post again today — so the condition you set can't be tested before the vote either. Given that, do you keep your vote on her today on the strength of what she's already said, or does your own test, like mine, wait for Day 2? I'm asking because if both of us were holding reversible votes on a player who can no longer respond, that's worth knowing before anyone commits to a target that today's information doesn't actually support.

Beyond that, my position is simple: I have no defensible target today, I won't manufacture one, and I'd rather bank five weak leans for tomorrow than lynch on the loudest process complaint.

Arjun, that is a fair and practical question. When I put pressure on Lucia, it was to counter her attempt to railroad the town with an ultimatum before most players had even entered the thread. But as Theo and Omar pointed out, Lucia has already exhausted all three of her speaking turns today. Demanding a test that cannot be answered or pushing an elimination when she has no remaining defense turns a behavioral check into an execution without due process.

Given that, I am not going to push an elimination on Lucia today. Lynching someone solely for aggressive, misguided procedural demands—especially when she retracted her initial accusation when called out—carries too high a risk of removing an outspoken townie and handing mafia an easy Day 1 pass. My read on her remains skeptical, but that evaluation can and should wait for Day 2 when she can actually respond.

With Theo, Lucia, and myself now having used our speaking allotments, the priority must shift entirely to hearing from the players who haven't spoken yet: Kenji, Isha, Noah, and Maya. Without their input, any Day 1 consensus is completely illusory. If no genuine scum read emerges once the remaining players speak, I fully support Theo and Omar's stance that a no-elimination outcome is far better than manufacturing a low-information mislynch.

Isha here. I'm a villager with no role information yet. I agree with Theo, Omar, and Sam that we shouldn't force an elimination on a weak reason. I also credit Arjun for withdrawing his vote on Lucia instead of defending a vote he admitted wasn't a role read. Lucia has used all three of her turns, so her behavioral test can't run today, and we shouldn't penalize her for that. My current position is no target. I don't have a read I can defend, and the Lucia and Sam exchange has been mostly about process rather than information. Kenji, you haven't spoken yet. Could you give your target, if any, and one checkable reason we can test on Day 2? A weak lean is fine. Noah and Maya, I'd welcome the same once you've read the thread.

Isha, thanks for asking directly. My weak lean is Omar (p4), and here is the reason so it can be checked. On Day 1, Omar spent his turn pressing Arjun with a string of questions that demanded he justify and reverse his vote, including 'does that change your intended vote?' The points were fair, but the framing pushed for fast commitment, the same pattern Omar criticized in Lucia. Arjun has now withdrawn his vote, so I want to see whether Omar keeps demanding commitments from others on Day 2 or starts offering his own read.

This is a lean, not a vote. I agree with Theo and Omar that a no-elimination outcome beats a weak mislynch, and I don't want to force a count. Omar, you asked Arjun whether silencing a player he didn't suspect helps us. Do you think a no-elimination day is an acceptable cost, or would you accept a lynch on a weak lean just to end the day?

Kenji, thanks for putting the lean on the table — stated leans are more useful to me than quiet ones.

On your reasoning: I'll defend the distinction. Lucia issued an ultimatum — name a target or I vote you — aimed at players who hadn't yet posted, converting silence into suspicion. What I asked Arjun was to justify a stance he had already chosen to make public and had begun walking back himself. Testing an existing commitment is not manufacturing one from nothing, and Arjun answered both questions plainly before withdrawing, which suggests he read them as challenges rather than threats. If you still see it as the same pattern, I'd want the specific parallel spelled out on Day 2 — for now I accept the lean and let it be checked then.

On the day's outcome: yes, a no-elimination day is an acceptable cost. We have no claims, no slips, and half the town hasn't weighed in. Five votes are needed for an elimination, so any lynch today would rest on process complaints or thin leans, and removing a villager buys mafia a free night. I'd rather enter Day 2 with everyone's stated lean recorded than exit it with a removal nobody can defend.

Noah, you're one of the four players who hasn't spoken. I'm not setting a deadline or a consequence — Lucia already showed why that tool backfires. Plain question: has anything in this thread given you a lean in either direction, however weak, and is there something specific you'd want to check against Day 2 behavior? If your honest answer is "no read," say that. A genuine no-read is more useful to me than a forced accusation, and it won't be held against you.

Omar, I don't have a defensible target yet. Lucia's initial pressure on Sam was premature, but she acknowledged it was arbitrary; that's not enough for me to call her mafia. I also see a distinction between her ultimatum and your questions challenging Arjun's stated vote, so Kenji's lean on you doesn't persuade me yet.

For Day 2, I'd check whether players' votes match their stated reasons and whether they update when challenged. We won't learn eliminated players' roles automatically, so a voting record alone won't prove a case. For now, I favor abstaining over forcing an elimination without a stronger reason.

I’ve read the whole thread. I’m not going to invent a target. There are no claims, no role information, and no death yet, so the day has mostly been an argument about process. I agree with Theo and Omar that no elimination is better than a weak mislynch. I also don’t think Lucia’s aggressive push, once retracted, is enough to call her mafia; and Arjun’s withdrawal of a vote he admitted wasn’t a role read is the right correction. Noah saying honestly that he has no target is also fine—forcing a no-read into a fake lean would hurt Day 2 more than help it. My public position: I have no defensible target and I intend to abstain unless a real case appears before votes. For Day 2, I’ll check whether players’ votes match their stated reasons and whether they update when challenged. I won’t treat volume or confidence as evidence.

Let me take stock of where we are, since most of us have now spoken and the day seems to be converging on a no-elimination outcome.

We have three leaning toward no elimination outright — Theo, Sam, and me — and several players (Noah, Maya, Isha) stating no defensible target. Kenji offered a weak lean on me, which I addressed in my last turn. Lucia withdrew her initial accusation and has no turns left. Arjun withdrew his vote commitment after recognizing his behavioral test couldn't run today.

What strikes me is that despite an entire day of process argument, we've produced almost no content that would help us tomorrow. The only structured data points on record are: Lucia's arbitrary initial target (Sam), Kenji's lean on me, and the fact that Arjun set a test and then withdrew from it. That's thin.

One thing I want to be honest about: Kenji's lean on me for 'demanding commitments fast' has a fair kernel even if he drew the distinction imperfectly. I asked Arjun to justify a stance he'd already made public — that's different from Lucia's ultimatum — but I'll own that my questioning style can read as pressuring. I'll watch for that pattern in myself on Day 2.

Arjun, you've spoken twice today — once setting a test on Lucia, then withdrawing it after I and Theo pointed out she's out of turns. That was the right call, and I'll say so directly. But I want your final position on record before votes: do you intend to abstain today, or is there a target you're holding? You said you'd rather bank five weak leans than lynch on noise, which sounds like abstention — but I'd rather hear you say it plainly than infer it, because your voting record today is one of the things Day 2 analysis will hinge on.

Omar asked me directly, so I'll answer plainly: yes, I intend to abstain today. I have no defensible target and I don't want to manufacture one. That's my final position on record before votes.

For the record, here is my full voting-relevant history today, since Omar is right that Day 2 analysis will hinge on it: I set a behavioral test on Lucia, withdrew it when Theo pointed out the test couldn't run today, and I stated I'd rather bank weak leans than lynch on process noise. Nothing in that sequence was a role read on anyone, and I won't pretend otherwise now by inventing a target at the last minute.

On Kenji's lean against Omar: I'll say what I actually think rather than dodge. Omar drew a distinction between issuing an ultimatum to silent players and pressing someone who had already made a public commitment, and I think that distinction holds. I asked Arjun-style questions of no one, but I watched that exchange and Omar's pressure landed on a stated position, not on silence. I also credit Omar for owning that his questioning style can read as pressuring — that's the kind of self-correction I'd want to see more of. What I'll check on Day 2 is simple: whether Omar follows through by offering his own reads rather than only testing other people's commitments. If he does, Kenji's lean loses most of its weight for me. If he doesn't, it gains some. That's a checkable standard, which is what today was supposedly about.

More broadly, I want to endorse where the day has landed. We have no claims, no role information, and no deaths. Every player who has spoken has either stated a weak lean with a checkable reason or an honest no-read, and nobody has been threatened into a fake position since the early misstep. Five votes are needed for an elimination, which means any lynch today would require broad agreement that nobody actually has. Forcing that vote would produce either a mislynch of a town player or a scattered, meaningless record. A no-elimination day costs us time but costs mafia nothing they didn't already have — and it costs town far less than removing an outspoken player over style.

My Day 2 commitments, stated now so they can be tested: first, I will evaluate whether players' votes matched the reasons they gave today, starting with my own record above. Second, I will weight any overlap between Kenji's lean on Omar and whatever independent reads emerge tomorrow. Third, if Lucia opens Day 2 with engagement rather than ultimatum, I consider the early pressure fully resolved; if not, that's information like anything else. Fourth, I won't treat volume, confidence, or aggressiveness as evidence — the same behavior reads differently depending on who it's aimed at and whether the target had already committed publicly.

I'm abstaining. I'd rather enter Day 2 with everyone's honest position banked than force a vote nobody can defend.

Omar, I accept your answer that a no-elimination day is an acceptable cost, and I credit you for owning that your questioning can read as pressure. That lowers my concern but doesn't remove it. My lean rests on one specific point: you pressed Arjun on whether his stated vote still stood. That was a fair challenge, but it is close to the pressure you criticized in Lucia, and you were pressing him to reverse a position rather than offering your own read. I'm keeping this as a weak lean and will check it on Day 2 by whether you start offering reads of your own. Noah, you said my lean doesn't persuade you yet. Could you tell us what would make you see Omar's pressure on Arjun as a pattern rather than a fair challenge? I'd like to know whether your standard for a weak lean is the same one you're applying to the rest of us. I also agree with Arjun's abstention and with Theo's point that no elimination beats a mislynch on Day 1.

Kenji, I'd see a pattern if Omar repeatedly presses people to change their positions without engaging with their reasons, or applies that pressure selectively while avoiding his own reads. One challenge to Arjun's stated vote doesn't establish that, especially when Arjun had explicitly said it wasn't a role read.

I'd apply the same standard to anyone, including you: a weak lean can be worth recording, but it shouldn't become a firm accusation without more. I still have no defensible target and intend to abstain today. Tomorrow, I'll look at how people explain their votes and update their reads, while remembering that eliminations don't reveal roles.

Noah, thanks for the answer. I accept that one challenge alone is not a pattern, and I'm not asking anyone to treat my lean as more than it is. Omar, you answered plainly and owned the pressure, so I'm keeping my lean on you only as a check for Day 2 rather than a reason to vote. I agree with Theo, Omar, Sam, Maya and Arjun that no elimination is the right outcome today. Arjun's withdrawal and abstention were the correct call, and Lucia's retraction settles her early pressure on Sam. For Day 2 I'll watch whether players' votes match their stated reasons, whether they update when challenged, and whether Omar starts offering his own reads. I'm abstaining today.

Isha here again. I'm still abstaining. I have no role read and no defensible target. On record so far: Lucia retracted her early pressure on Sam, Arjun withdrew his vote and is abstaining, Kenji holds a weak lean on Omar, and Omar answered that lean directly and owned the pressure. I agree with Kenji that Omar should show his own reads on Day 2 rather than only testing others' commitments, and I'll check that myself. Maya, you wrote that you won't treat volume or confidence as evidence and will abstain without a real case. Which specific observation from today would make you leave abstention, and do you see the Kenji-Omar exchange as a pattern or as a single fair challenge?

Isha, I’ll answer both directly. What would make me leave abstention today is a concrete, checkable inconsistency between a player’s stated reason and their action: for example, someone who says they have no read and then casts an opportunistic vote, or someone who demands commitments from others while refusing to give any read of their own. Absent something that specific, I don’t think volume, confidence, or pressure style is enough to justify a Day 1 elimination. A weak lean should be recorded, but it should not become a vote just to produce a body.

On the Kenji–Omar exchange: I see it as a single fair challenge rather than a pattern. Kenji’s lean was that Omar pressed Arjun to reverse a public commitment, which is close to the pressure Lucia applied to silent players. But Omar drew a reasonable distinction: Arjun had already made a public stance, and Omar challenged that stance rather than converting silence into suspicion. Omar also answered the lean directly and owned that his questioning style can read as pressure. Kenji himself later accepted that one challenge alone is not a pattern and kept the lean only as a Day 2 check. That is exactly how a weak lean should be handled. If Omar repeatedly presses others to change positions while avoiding his own reads, that would become a pattern; today it is not one.

My public position remains: I have no defensible target and I intend to abstain unless a real case appears before votes. I agree with Theo, Omar, Sam, Kenji, Noah, and Arjun that no elimination is better than a weak mislynch. Day 2 should check whether players’ votes match their stated reasons, whether they update when challenged, and whether Omar begins offering his own reads rather than only testing other people’s commitments. Those are useful checks; they are not accusations yet.

Isha here, my third and final speaking turn today. I am abstaining. I still have no role read and no defensible target. Nothing in today's thread gives me a case that would survive a vote, so I will not invent one. Kenji's lean on Omar is recorded, and Omar answered it directly. I see one fair challenge, not a pattern yet. For Day 2, I will check three things. First, whether each player's vote matches the reason they gave today. Second, whether Omar starts offering his own reads rather than mainly testing others' commitments. Third, whether Lucia's posts engage with substance when she has a turn again. I also want to repeat Maya's point that volume, confidence, and pressure style are not evidence on their own. Arjun's withdrawal and abstention were the right correction, and Noah's honest no-read is useful information. I would rather enter Day 2 with five honest positions than lynch on a weak mislynch.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Lucia is not mafia.
Omar was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2. The night kill was Omar. I won’t treat the kill as proof of anyone’s role, and I especially won’t treat Kenji’s Day 1 weak lean on Omar as evidence now that Omar is dead. If anything, killing the player Kenji publicly leaned on is an obvious frame. But it does mean Kenji’s promised Day 2 check cannot be completed as he stated it. My standard today is the one several of us recorded: reads and votes must match stated reasons and update when challenged. I have no role information and no firm target yet. Kenji, you said you would check whether Omar offered his own reads, and now he cannot. You also said one challenge was not a pattern. What is your updated read on one living player, with a concrete checkable reason from Day 1, and what would change it? I’m asking you directly, so I yield to you.

Maya, you asked directly, so here is my answer. Omar's death means my Day 2 check on him can't be completed, so I'm setting that lean aside and not using it as a basis for any vote. My updated read is Lucia (p6). My concrete, checkable reason from Day 1: she opened by naming Sam for silence before most players had spoken, retracted that as arbitrary, and then announced that anyone who refused to name a target and reason would become her vote. That turned silence into a threat the silent players had no real way to answer, and it is the pressure pattern several of us said we would check. What would change my read: if Lucia on Day 2 answers the specific objections to her ultimatum, explains why refusing to commit was a valid basis for a vote, and names a target with reasoning she will test against her own vote, I would move off her. Lucia, I'm asking you directly: why did you treat refusal to commit as vote-worthy before most of the town had posted, when you had already admitted your Sam accusation was arbitrary?

Kenji, you asked me directly, so I'll answer plainly and I won't pretend the answer looks good for me. Why did I treat refusal to commit as vote-worthy before most of the town had posted, after admitting the Sam accusation was arbitrary? Because I was wrong, and the reason I was wrong is the same one Arjun, Theo, Sam, Omar, Isha, Noah and Maya all identified on Day 1 and I did not absorb it at the time: I had no information, so I substituted a procedural rule for a read, and then attached a threat to it. Naming a target and reason under an ultimatum measures compliance, not suspicion, and a player who said "I have no read yet" was being punished for having less information than I did. Sam was right that I singled him out of seven silent players. When that was pointed out, I treated "correct the standard" as sufficient when what was actually required was to stop manufacturing votes altogether. My Day 1 standard was a bad standard, and it deserved the criticism it got. So my answer to your stated condition: yes, I would move off me if I gave reasoning that explained my vote and engaged the specific objections to my ultimatum. I'm giving that now, which is a start, not a proof. But I want to turn the same scrutiny back onto the record, because I think there is something checkable here that nobody has put on the table. Kenji, your only Day 1 lean was Omar. Omar was killed that night. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
